desc:
A ticker receives price records out of order and sometimes corrects an earlier record. ops is a list of triples [type, a, b]:

  • [1, t, price]: record that the price at timestamp t is price. If timestamp t was recorded before, this replaces the old price (a correction).
  • [2, 0, 0]: report the price at the latest timestamp recorded so far.
  • [3, 0, 0]: report the maximum of the current prices over all timestamps.
  • [4, 0, 0]: report the minimum of the current prices over all timestamps.

The first operation is always a record. Return the answers to all queries (types 2, 3 and 4) in order.

ops = [[1,1,10], [1,2,5], [3,0,0], [4,0,0], [1,1,3], [3,0,0], [4,0,0], [2,0,0], [1,4,2], [2,0,0], [4,0,0]]
prices: t1=10, t2=5  -> max 10, min 5
correct t1 to 3      -> max 5, min 3, latest (t2) 5
record t4=2          -> latest 2, min 2
answer = [10, 5, 5, 3, 5, 2, 2]
constraints: Every query is preceded by at least one record
hints: A hash map from timestamp to its current price handles records, corrections and the latest-timestamp query. The max and min queries are the hard ones.
A heap can give the max or min quickly, but a correction changes a price that is already inside the heap, and you cannot easily delete from the middle of one.

Do not delete. On every record push (price, t) into a max-heap and a min-heap. When a query looks at the top, discard it while its price differs from the current price of that timestamp (it is stale), then read the top.
editorial: Keep price[t] (the current value) and the largest timestamp seen. The latest price is just price[latest].

For max and min use two heaps with lazy deletion. Every record pushes an entry (price, t) into both heaps. A correction does not remove the old entry; instead, when a query inspects the top of a heap, it checks whether the entry still matches price[t]. If not, the entry is stale and is popped; this repeats until the top is current. The top is then the true extreme. If a stale entry happens to equal the current price again (the value was corrected back), it is simply valid, which is harmless.

Each entry is pushed once and popped at most once, so all operations cost O(log n) amortised and the total is O(n log n). The lazy-deletion pattern is the standard answer whenever a heap must support updates or deletions of arbitrary elements.
